title: What is a Financial Model?
subtitle: The analyst's financial forecasting tool
openingQuestion: What is a financial model used for?
openingOptions: Forecasting the future: revenue, cost, cash flow to inform investment, M&A, and valuation decisions
explanation: A financial model is an Excel/Google Sheets spreadsheet that simulates a company's financial operations based on assumptions. Used for: DCF valuation, LBO analysis, M&A accretion/dilution, budget planning. The 3-statement model is the foundation: P&L → Balance Sheet → Cash Flow, all linked together.

diagram.label: Used for DCF, LBO, M&A, budgeting

realWorldExample.company: The financial model behind VinFast's IPO valuation
realWorldExample.description: Before VinFast's IPO, investment banks and analysts built detailed financial models forecasting electric vehicle sales, profit margins, and capital needs for factory investment over many years ahead, in order to arrive at a reasonable valuation for the IPO.

quiz.question: What does the 3-statement model consist of, and how are they linked?
options: The P&L flows into the balance sheet and the cash flow statement
The three statements are built independently and then reconciled at period end
The balance sheet drives the P&L, while cash flow is calculated separately
Three separate forecasts of the company's revenue, cost, and profit
quiz.explanation: Net income from the P&L → adds to Retained Earnings in the BS. Depreciation from the P&L → added back in CFO. CapEx → subtracted in CFO, added to PP&E in the BS. Debt issuance → CFF and Notes Payable. The three statements are tightly linked.

quiz.question: Why is a linked 3-statement financial model considered a mandatory foundation before doing DCF valuation or LBO analysis?
options: Because DCF only runs when there's enough data from the last five years
Because every assumption change must flow correctly through all three statements
Because investment banks require submitting all three statements during due diligence
Because the balance sheet is the only source for free cash flow
quiz.explanation: A professional financial model must guarantee "articulation" - every changed assumption (e.g. revenue growth) must automatically flow through all three linked statements accurately; this is the foundation of every valuation analysis.

quiz.question: What signals that a financial model has a linkage error?
options: Margin stays constant across the entire forecast period
Forecast revenue grows faster than the industry average
The balance sheet doesn't balance after changing one assumption
Free cash flow is negative in the first two years of a project
quiz.explanation: Assets must always equal liabilities plus equity in every scenario. Being off by even one unit means some line hasn't been linked correctly - and every number downstream, including the valuation result, becomes unusable.

quiz.question: Why is depreciation added back in the cash flow statement?
options: Because it's recorded on the balance sheet rather than the P&L
Because it was already deducted twice at the pre-tax profit line
Because it gets refunded when the business liquidates the asset
Because it's an accounting charge, not actual cash going out
quiz.explanation: The real cash outflow happens when the asset is purchased (CapEx); depreciation just allocates that cost across many years. Starting from net income means it has to be added back since it never actually left the till.

quiz.question: Which assumption gets sensitivity-tested the most in a model?
options: Revenue growth and the discount rate
The number of public holidays in the forecast fiscal year
The exchange rate used to convert year-end statements
The average salary of the back-office staff
quiz.explanation: These two assumptions drive most of the result and are also the two places most prone to error. A serious model always includes a two-way sensitivity table for them, since a single number always creates a false sense of certainty.

practicePrompt.question: An analyst builds an Excel spreadsheet forecasting a company's revenue, costs, and profit over the next 5 years, based on assumptions about growth rate, margin, and interest rate on debt. What is this tool called?
options: A financial model forecasts the financials from assumptions, supporting valuation and decisions
This is called a Balance Sheet, because the spreadsheet contains the company's asset and liability figures
This is called an Audit Report, because the spreadsheet checks the accuracy of already-published financial statements
This is just a plain spreadsheet with no specific technical name in finance
practicePrompt.explanation: Financial model: forecasting finances based on assumptions. This is the core tool in corporate finance and investing - the forecast result (revenue, profit, cash flow) is only as reliable as the quality of the input assumptions (growth, margin, interest rate...).

application.title: Try building a simple model
application.message: Open a spreadsheet and try forecasting your income and spending for the next 3 months based on a few assumptions (a salary raise, fixed spending) - that is itself a small-scale financial model.
application.secondary: No need for complex formulas, just build the habit of forecasting with clear assumptions.

sections.text: The Financial Model is the central tool of every financial analyst - a spreadsheet simulating a company's financial operations based on assumptions, used for valuation, forecasting, and investment decisions.
The 3-statement model: the foundation of every financial model

A 3-statement model links three financial statements together: the P&L (Net Income) flows into the Balance Sheet (increasing Retained Earnings) and into the Cash Flow Statement (starting from Net Income). Depreciation from the P&L is added back in operating cash flow (CFO). CapEx is subtracted in CFO but increases PP&E on the Balance Sheet. New debt issuance appears in financing cash flow (CFF) and increases Notes Payable on the Balance Sheet. The three statements are linked so tightly that changing one small assumption ripples through all three.
Why the 3-statement model is mandatory before DCF and LBO

Both DCF valuation and LBO analysis need an accurate free cash flow (FCF) forecast - and FCF can only be calculated correctly when the three financial statements are consistently linked, ensuring every change in one statement is properly reflected in the other two (a property called 'articulation'). Before VinFast's IPO, investment banks and analysts had to build detailed financial models forecasting electric vehicle sales, profit margins, and factory investment capital needs over many years to arrive at a well-founded valuation for the IPO.

items: 3-statement model: P&L → Balance Sheet → Cash Flow Statement, tightly linked together
**Applications:** DCF valuation, LBO analysis, M&A accretion/dilution analysis, internal budget planning
A good model must have 'articulation' - every changed assumption must automatically flow accurately through all three statements
The model's quality determines the reliability of every valuation conclusion drawn from it

lines: A financial model is only as good as the quality of the assumptions fed into it - 'garbage in, garbage out' applies here absolutely.
